- **mise + air-gapped/policy-restricted networks** - mise's `aqua` backend verifies tflint/trivy via cosign + GitHub artifact attestations, which reach `sigstore.dev`/`tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev`; a `terraform` exact pin instead downloads straight from HashiCorp (no sigstore). If a sandbox blocks sigstore, exact-version installs of aqua tools fail there even though GitHub-hosted CI succeeds - it is an egress limitation, not a config defect.
- **Validate before merge** - `npx --package renovate renovate-config-validator .github/renovate.json` catches schema errors locally; the Mend app uses the in-repo config (no onboarding PR) once present.

## Custom conditions (precondition / postcondition / check)

- **A `check` earns its place only on a fact Terraform does NOT manage** - asserting on a managed
  attribute is dead weight: the drift already surfaces as a resource diff, and the pending change
  makes Terraform defer the check to apply time (`Check block assertion known after apply`), by
  which point the apply has reconciled the very thing the check was watching. Found the hard way on
  a `key_state == "Enabled"` assertion over `aws_kms_key.is_enabled`; the check never fired once.
- **A scoped data source is invisible outside its own check**, so anything a resource consumes needs
  a second, top-level lookup. That duplication is a feature, not a smell: the top-level read feeds
  the configuration, the scoped read observes reality on every run.
- **Use the plural data source for optional lookups** - `aws_iam_roles` returns an empty set where
  `aws_iam_role` errors and fails the plan. That difference is what lets one module deploy across
  accounts at different baseline stages.
- **Gate versus signal is a governance call, not a technical one.** Same assertion machinery, same
  kind of fact; what changes is the verdict you are willing to hand down. State the policy reason in
  the `error_message`, not just the condition.

## AWS gotchas

- **Deleting an IAM principal referenced in a resource policy freezes it as its unique ID** - AWS
  rewrites the ARN to `AROA...` rather than dropping the entry, because the ARN only resolves while
  the principal exists. Recreating the role mints a *new* unique ID, so the policy AWS holds and the
  policy Terraform renders genuinely differ until the next apply. Expect one extra apply after any
  role recreation.
- **A KMS key in active use can still be disabled or scheduled for deletion** - AWS does not track
  whether a key is in use and blocks nothing. Disabling a key that encrypts a live S3 bucket is
  accepted immediately; the bucket then fails `PutObject` with `KMS.DisabledException`.
- **An organization-perimeter `Deny` needs `BoolIfExists aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`** - AWS service
  principals carry no `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, so `StringNotEquals` matches them and the deny takes out
  the service that was supposed to use the key. And since a `Deny` in a key policy also governs who
  may edit that policy, a miscalibrated condition leaves the key unrecoverable: validate on a
  throwaway key, and keep the statement behind a variable.

## Local environment

- **A local DNS filter that blackholes `logs.*` stops any example creating a log group** - the
  resolver answers `0.0.0.0` for `logs.<region>.amazonaws.com`, so the apply dies with
  `dial tcp 0.0.0.0:443: connect: connection refused` on `aws_cloudwatch_log_group` and leaves a
  partial state: everything up to the log group is created, the log group and whatever depends on
  it are not. `dig @1.1.1.1` does not settle it - a filtering router intercepts port 53 to public
  resolvers too. Compare the system resolver against DoH instead:
  `curl -H 'accept: application/dns-json' 'https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?name=logs.<region>.amazonaws.com&type=A'`.
  Work around it with `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_CLOUDWATCH_LOGS=https://logs.<region>.api.aws`, the
  dual-stack name, which is not caught by the `logs.` prefix rule.
- **An environment workaround belongs in the example README, not in the operator's shell** - the
  one above was documented in `terraform-actions-lambda` only, so the next example creating a log
  group (`terraform-secrets-out-of-state`) hit the exact same wall from scratch, on demo day. Any
  example that creates an `aws_cloudwatch_log_group` carries the `## Troubleshooting` bullet.
  Duplication across examples is the intended cost of self-contained examples.

- **An organization-perimeter `Deny` needs `BoolIfExists aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`** - AWS service
  principals carry no `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, so `StringNotEquals` matches them and the deny takes out
  the service that was supposed to use the key. And since a `Deny` in a key policy also governs who
  may edit that policy, a miscalibrated condition leaves the key unrecoverable: validate on a
  throwaway key, and keep the statement behind a variable.

Fait. Sans commit.

## Ce que j'ai changé après le live précédent : rien de durable

La parade n'a été posée que dans `terraform-actions-lambda/README.md`. Rien dans `tasks/lessons.md`, rien dans `AGENTS.md`, rien dans ce lab-ci. Elle ne survivait que dans un `export` de shell — donc elle s'évapore entre deux sessions, et le lab suivant qui crée un log group se reprend le mur. C'est ça la récidive, pas le DNS.

## Sur la validation : ta prémisse est à corriger sur un point

L'empreinte mesurée aujourd'hui au palier 1 est `24437ec9` — exactement la première des trois notées le 2026-08-11. Le consommateur **avait** donc bien tourné ce jour-là, avec l'`export` en place dans ce shell. Ce qui n'a jamais été fait, c'est de sortir la parade du shell. Et la note du live cochait « Parade DNS documentée » pour ce lab, où elle ne l'était pas : c'est la case fausse qui a masqué le trou.

## Validation bout en bout (aujourd'hui, sandbox eu-west-1)

| Geste | Mesure |
|---|---|
| apply avec parade | log group créé en 1s, 3 ressources ajoutées |
| palier 1 | secret en clair dans le state, empreinte `24437ec9` |
| palier 5 | plan = update in-place, `secret_string -> null`, `secret_string_wo` absent |
| état après 5 | `secret_string: ""`, `has_secret_string_wo: true` |
| 5 → 6 **sans** bump | **`No changes`** — la valeur générée ne part pas |
| bump en 2 | `forces replacement`, 1 add / 1 destroy, empreinte `49887fae` |
| étiquettes | `AWSCURRENT` / `AWSPREVIOUS`, aucun résidu |

Toutes les affirmations du README tiennent. Le `No changes` au 5→6 est nouveau : le no-op silencieux est jouable au terminal au lieu d'être annoncé en slide.

## Changes

`terraform-examples` (branche `feat/terraform-secrets-out-of-state`, PR #46) :
- `tasks/lessons.md` — nouvelle section `## Local environment` : le symptôme, le diagnostic DoH (pourquoi `dig @1.1.1.1` ne tranche pas), la parade, et la leçon « ça vit dans le README de l'exemple, pas dans le shell »
- `AGENTS.md` — golden path : `## Troubleshooting` obligatoire pour tout exemple qui crée un `aws_cloudwatch_log_group`
- `secret.tf` restauré au palier 1, identique à HEAD

Note du live, 4 endroits : titre « Vérifié » + bullet de la passe du 12/08 · conséquence conducteur HOW-3 · case ligne 220 corrigée · Pré-vol : l'`export` en première étape avec son contrôle `dig`. Linter éditorial vert.

## Deux choses pour toi

**La sandbox est restée déployée** au palier 6 (version 2, mot de passe aléatoire). Le `terraform destroy` m'a été refusé par le classifier. Le pré-vol demande un reset — dis-moi et je le lance, ou fais-le toi :
```
export AWS_PROFILE=sandbox AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_CLOUDWATCH_LOGS=https://logs.eu-west-1.api.aws
mise exec -- terraform destroy
```

**Une autre session écrit dans les mêmes fichiers.** Le `## Troubleshooting` du README du lab n'est pas de moi (absent de mon grep initial, présent ensuite), et une phrase dupliquée est apparue dans la note pendant que j'éditais — je l'ai dédupliquée. Le `git diff` du vault montre aussi 6 fichiers touchés que je n'ai pas ouverts. Vérifie l'index avant de committer.

1	"""Consume a secret by ARN and prove which value is current, without ever revealing it.
2	
3	The function reads the secret at runtime through SECRET_ARN. Terraform never handles
4	the value: it only wires the ARN. What comes back is a fingerprint - enough to see a
5	rotation happen, useless to anyone who intercepts it.
6	
7	Two sinks, so the demo never depends on a third party being reachable:
8	
9	- `stdout` (default) returns the fingerprint and the message it would have sent.
10	- `twitch` exchanges the refresh token for an access token and posts to a chat.
11	  This is the realistic shape: what rests in the vault is the durable refresh
12	  token, and the short-lived access token is derived at each call and kept nowhere.
13	"""
14	
15	import hashlib
16	import json
17	import os
18	import urllib.parse
19	import urllib.request
20

file.content:
"""Consume a secret by ARN and prove which value is current, without ever revealing it.

The function reads the secret at runtime through SECRET_ARN. Terraform never handles
the value: it only wires the ARN. What comes back is a fingerprint - enough to see a
rotation happen, useless to anyone who intercepts it.

Two sinks, so the demo never depends on a third party being reachable:

- `stdout` (default) returns the fingerprint and the message it would have sent.
- `twitch` exchanges the refresh token for an access token and posts to a chat.
  This is the realistic shape: what rests in the vault is the durable refresh
  token, and the short-lived access token is derived at each call and kept nowhere.
"""

import hashlib
import json
import os
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request

import boto3

_secrets = boto3.client("secretsmanager")

_TOKEN_URL = "https://id.twitch.tv/oauth2/token"
_CHAT_URL = "https://api.twitch.tv/helix/chat/messages"


def _fingerprint(value: str) -> str:
    """First 8 hex chars of the SHA-256 digest. One-way, and short enough to read aloud."""
    return hashlib.sha256(value.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:8]


def _post(url: str, data: bytes, headers: dict) -> dict:
    request = urllib.request.Request(url, data=data, headers=headers, method="POST")
    with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=8) as response:
        return json.loads(response.read())


def _refresh_access_token(creds: dict) -> str:
    """Trade the durable refresh token for a short-lived access token, kept in memory only."""
    body = urllib.parse.urlencode(
        {
            "client_id": creds["client_id"],
            "client_secret": creds["client_secret"],
            "refresh_token": creds["refresh_token"],
            "grant_type": "refresh_token",
        }
    ).encode()
    headers = {"Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"}
    return _post(_TOKEN_URL, body, headers)["access_token"]


def _send_chat_message(creds: dict, user_id: str, message: str) -> None:
    access_token = _refresh_access_token(creds)
    body = json.dumps(
        {"broadcaster_id": user_id, "sender_id": user_id, "message": message}
    ).encode()
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {access_token}",
        "Client-Id": creds["client_id"],
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
    }
    _post(_CHAT_URL, body, headers)


def handler(event, context):  # noqa: ARG001 - Lambda signature
    secret_arn = os.environ["SECRET_ARN"]
    sink = os.environ.get("SINK", "stdout")

    secret = _secrets.get_secret_value(SecretId=secret_arn)["SecretString"]

    # The secret is a JSON credential set. Only the refresh token is fingerprinted:
    # it is the field a rotation actually changes.
    try:
        creds = json.loads(secret)
        token = creds["refresh_token"]
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError):
        # A step-1 secret may still be a bare string. Fingerprint it as-is.
        creds, token = {}, secret

    label = (event or {}).get("label", "current secret")
    fingerprint = _fingerprint(token)
    message = f"{label} -> fingerprint {fingerprint}"

    if sink == "stdout":
        print(message)
        return {"sink": sink, "fingerprint": fingerprint, "message": message}

    if sink == "twitch":
        _send_chat_message(creds, os.environ["TWITCH_USER_ID"], message)
        return {"sink": sink, "fingerprint": fingerprint, "sent": True}

    raise ValueError(f"unknown SINK: {sink}")

Normal. Le fichier de sortie de `aws lambda invoke` contient **la valeur de retour du handler**, pas le stdout de la fonction.

Trois canaux distincts :

| Ce que fait le code | Où ça sort |
|---|---|
| `return {"sink", "fingerprint", "message"}` | le fichier de sortie (`/dev/stdout` ici) |
| `print(message)` | CloudWatch Logs, jamais dans la réponse |
| — | `StatusCode`/`ExecutedVersion` = métadonnées du CLI, sur son propre stdout |

`SINK=stdout` dans ce lab veut dire « renvoie l'empreinte dans la réponse plutôt que de la poster sur Twitch ». Ça ne veut pas dire « le CLI t'affiche le stdout de la fonction ». Le `print()` de la ligne 87 part en logs, point.

Donc le hash arrive bien, par le retour : `{"sink": "stdout", "fingerprint": "24437ec9", "message": "..."}` — collé devant le bloc `StatusCode` sans newline, ce qui le rend facile à rater à l'écran.

Si tu veux voir le `print()` : `--log-type Tail --query LogResult --output text | base64 -d`.

1	# ===========================================================================
2	# THE ONLY FILE THAT MOVES.
3	#
4	# This root module is a PROGRESSIVE LAB, and it starts on the anti-pattern.
5	# Do not copy this file as a reference - copy `final/` instead, which holds the
6	# target state alone.
7	#
8	# Six steps. Exactly one is active at a time: uncomment the next, comment the
9	# previous, and run the proof command from the README. Steps 3 and 4 fail on
10	# purpose - that is what they teach, so they can never be the active step in CI.
11	#
12	# Every value in this lab is throwaway.
13	# ===========================================================================
14	
15	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
16	# STEP 1 - the plain variable. Where most configurations still are.
17	#
18	# Read the plan first: `secret_string` already shows as `(sensitive value)`,
19	# because the AWS provider marks that attribute Sensitive in its own schema.
20	# Nothing has been configured, and the plan already looks safe. That is the trap.
21	#
22	# Proof: see `state_proof_command` in outputs.tf. The token is there, in clear.
23	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
24	variable "api_token" {
25	  description = "Throwaway credential set, JSON encoded. Never a real secret."
26	  type        = string
27	  default     = "{\"client_id\":\"dummy-client-id\",\"client_secret\":\"dummy-client-secret\",\"refresh_token\":\"dummy-refresh-token-v1\"}"
28	  sensitive = true
29	}
30	
31	resource "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "app" {
32	  secret_id     = aws_secretsmanager_secret.app.id
33	  secret_string = var.api_token
34	}
35	
36	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
37	# STEP 2 - sensitive values. The reflex, and why it is not enough.
38	# Add `sensitive = true` to the variable above, then re-run the same proof.
39	# The state has not moved one byte.
40	#
41	# What `sensitive` actually buys is not the plan (the provider already masked
42	# that attribute) but everywhere else the value travels: outputs, locals, other
43	# resources, error messages.
44	#
45	# The contagion, worth seeing once: a derived output stops the plan with
46	# "Output refers to sensitive values" until it is marked sensitive too. In a
47	# reusable module that spreads across the whole public interface.
48	#
49	# output "token_preview" {
50	#   value = var.api_token
51	# }
52	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
53	
54	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
55	# STEP 3 - ephemeral argument. The wall, and the clearest error in Terraform.
56	# Add `ephemeral = true` to the variable, keep `secret_string` above, then plan:
57	#
58	#   Error: Invalid use of ephemeral value
59	#
60	#   Ephemeral values are not valid for "secret_string", because it is not a
61	#   write-only attribute and must be persisted to state.
62	#
63	# The value can no longer reach the state, and it has nowhere to land either.
64	# `ephemeral` brings a secret in. It cannot write it.
65	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
66	
67	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
68	# STEP 4 - ephemeral block. The other source, and its usage restriction.
69	# A classic `data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version"` puts the value back in the
70	# state on a plain READ. The ephemeral block does not.
71	#
72	# ephemeral "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "current" {
73	#   secret_id = aws_secretsmanager_secret.app.id
74	# }
75	#
76	# Referencing it outside an ephemeral context stops the plan:
77	#
78	#   Error: Ephemeral value not allowed
79	#
80	#   This output value is not declared as returning an ephemeral value, so it
81	#   cannot be set to a result derived from an ephemeral value.
82	#
83	# output "current_token" {
84	#   value = ephemeral.aws_secretsmanager_secret_version.current.secret_string
85	# }
86	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
87	
88	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
89	# STEP 5 - write-only argument. The landing strip, and the migration.
90	#
91	# Switching an EXISTING resource from `secret_string` to `secret_string_wo` is
92	# an in-place update. The plan shows `secret_string -> null` plus the new version
93	# argument, and `secret_string_wo` never appears - write-only values are absent
94	# from plans by design. The value is still transmitted (verified on this
95	# resource, see README "Migrating an existing secret").
96	#
97	# After apply the state holds has_secret_string_wo = true and an EMPTY
98	# secret_string. The current state is clean; earlier state versions are not.
99	#
100	# resource "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "app" {
101	#   secret_id                = aws_secretsmanager_secret.app.id
102	#   secret_string_wo         = var.api_token
103	#   secret_string_wo_version = 1
104	# }
105	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
106	
107	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
108	# STEP 6 - generated in place. A secret nobody has ever seen.
109	# Terraform generates it, hands it to the vault through the write-only argument,
110	# and keeps nothing. Consumers read it by ARN. No human is ever in the loop.
111	#
112	# Rotation is the version bump. The plan reads:
113	#   ~ secret_string_wo_version = 1 -> 2 # forces replacement

Le README dit aujourd'hui que les commandes de preuve sont émises en outputs « so they can be pasted rather than typed », et le bloc `## Run` montre la forme `eval`. Ce qui manque, c'est le seul geste qui casse : `terraform output <nom>` sans `-raw` — c'est le réflexe naturel du lecteur, et tu viens de te le prendre. Une clause suffit :

> Proof commands are emitted as outputs (`state_proof_command`, `fingerprint_command`) so they can be pasted rather than typed. **Read them with `-raw`: a plain `terraform output` reprints the value HCL-escaped, and the pasted jq will not compile.**

Le reste — pourquoi un fichier plutôt que `/dev/stdout` — n'a pas sa place dans le README : le lecteur exécute la commande, il n'a pas à connaître le détail. Il est au bon endroit, dans le commentaire de `outputs.tf`.
